chunk_findings.detail: The new `check_budget_s` documentation promises that `ddflow doctor` “times each of its checks,” but the implementation only instruments a hardcoded subset of checks in `ddflow/api/reporting/health.py`. Several potentially expensive checks remain outside any `_check(...)` block, including `_rules_findings(...)` and `_launcher_findings(...)` around lines 436–438, `_driver_drift_notes`/`PM.driver_notes`/`PM.hook_notes` around line 441, `_unknown_author_notes` and `RP.doctor_notes` around lines 445–446, the `CL.unclaimed_trees` loop around line 457, `_untitled`, `_dupe_note`, and `cost.notes()` around line 474. If one of those untimed checks is the actual slow one on the 116 MB log — for example, if `RP.doctor_notes(...)` takes 10 minutes — then `timings` has no entry for it, `over_budget` remains empty, and `ddflow doctor` can still exceed 14 minutes while the new diagnostic reports that no check exceeded `check_budget_s`. That defeats the stated per-check timing/regression goal for any slow check not manually wrapped.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/health.py:48

chunk_findings.detail: `test_a_check_under_budget_is_not_reported` never configures `[health].check_budget_s`, so the test does not actually put the check under a known budget. It runs the real `embed` check and asserts it is not over budget based on whatever ambient/default budget and machine timing happen to be. On a loaded CI machine, cold filesystem, or with a default budget lower than the real embed check, the test can fail even when the over-budget feature is correct; with no default budget, the assertion can be vacuously true without exercising the under-budget path.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_doctor_time.py:39

chunk_findings.detail: The test file’s docstring promises that an over-budget check is reported “in `over_budget` (and as a note)”, but the test only checks that some `over_budget` entry contains the substring `"embed"`. It never asserts that the corresponding note is emitted or has the expected content, so a change that records `over_budget` but omits or corrupts the user-facing note would still pass this test.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_doctor_time.py:35

chunk_findings.detail: `_over_budget_notes` is defined but never called in `doctor` (or anywhere else in this file): `timings` is populated by `_check`, but after the wrapped calls it is not appended to `notes`, returned, or rendered. Running doctor on a log where one of the timed checks exceeds the configured budget therefore produces the same report as before: no “doctor check … over the budget” note and no timing table. The helpers and config can pass their tests while the user-visible falsifier remains true.

chunk_findings.detail: The instrumentation does not cover all doctor work. For example `SM.accept(repo, log)` when `accept_lost_events` is true, `RULEVIEW.notes(repo, cfg, st)`, `OVR.notes(events, st, cfg)`, `AUD.findings(st, cfg)`, and `fold_problem_notes(st)` are executed without `_check`. On a log where one of those is the 14-minute consumer, there is no timing row for it, so the per-check budget table cannot name the slow check, contrary to the stated “timing every check” intent.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `check_budget_s` knob promises that “ddflow doctor times each of its checks” and records per-check timings, but several checks in this same function are still executed outside any `_check` context: `_rules_findings(repo, st.highest_version, problems, notes)`, `_launcher_findings(...)`, `PM.driver_notes(...)`, `RP.doctor_notes(...)`, and `CL.unclaimed_trees(...)`, among others. A repo with many workflow definitions or many worktrees can make one of those exceed the configured budget, yet it will produce no row in `check_timings` and no over-budget note at all. In that input the promised diagnostic output remains empty even though doctor blows its budget, so the change does not meet its own per-check timing promise.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/health.py `_rules_findings` and `_launcher_findings`

chunk_findings.detail: The over-budget test calls `run_cli(repo, "init")` and then appends a second `[health]` table to the generated `.ddflow/config.toml`. Since this change adds the `[health]` section via `ddflow/config_sections/health.py`, `ddflow init` emits a `[health]` table; the appended `[health]` table makes the TOML invalid because TOML forbids redefining a table. When `reporting.doctor` loads the config, Python 3.11+ `tomllib` raises `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`, so the regression test cannot reach the monkeypatch/timing assertions in the normal initialized repository.

chunk_findings.detail:
The helper still appends a second `[health]` table to `.ddflow/config.toml` after `ddflow init` has already generated the default config. Because this change ships a `[health]` config section (`ddflow/config_sections/health.py`), the generated config contains a `[health]` table; appending `"
[health]

"` creates a duplicate TOML table. On Python 3.11+, `tomllib` (used when loading the config) rejects duplicate table definitions, so both `test_a_check_over_its_budget_is_reported` and `test_a_check_under_budget_is_not_reported` can fail with `TOMLDecodeError` before the monkeypatched embed check or over-budget logic is exercised. The rewrite of the test did not remove the duplicate-table defect; it moved it into `_set_budget`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new assertion only verifies that *some* note contains the literal `"over the 1s per-check budget"`; it does not tie that note to the over-budget `embed` entry. If the implementation records `embed` in `out.data["over_budget"]` but fails to emit the corresponding user-facing note, the test still passes whenever any other un-stubbed, real check (e.g., `log-read` or `plan`) happens to exceed the 1-second budget on a loaded CI runner and produces the same phrase. The regression test therefore does not reliably fail when the falsifying bug — an over-budget check not reported to the user — occurs.

chunk_findings.detail: The change implements the refusal path but not the promised explicit override path. `unknown_needs()` is called unconditionally in both add paths and in `update`; nothing in the changed code threads or honors an override flag. For example, the documented escape hatch from the acceptance criteria (`ddflow task add Tx --title t --needs NOPE-123 --force`, or the equivalent explicit flag) still returns `O.failed` because line 78/254 calls `IT.unknown_needs(...)` before any bypass, and `_edit.py:195` does the same for `--needs`/`--add-needs`. Thus the behavior is “always refuse,” not “refuse unless an explicit flag is given,” which fails the stated requirement that override be possible only with an explicit flag.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_add.py:78 (and :254; also ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:195)

chunk_findings.detail: These refusal tests assert only that the CLI exits non-zero and echoes the bad id; they do not assert that the queue was left unchanged. For example, if `task add T --title t --needs NO-SUCH-ID` creates task `T`, then prints an error and returns 1, lines 18-20 pass even though the command did not “refuse” in the intended sense. The same weakness applies to `update T --add-needs GHOST` and `update T --needs A,GHOST`: an implementation that mutates dependencies before validation can leave `GHOST` recorded or otherwise corrupt the item and still pass because only exit status/message are checked.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:16

chunk_findings.detail: `test_task_add_names_the_nearest_real_id` does not actually verify that the nearest real id is named. With tasks `A` and `B` present, it only asserts that the output contains the substring `"Did you mean"`. A CLI that prints `"Did you mean B?"` or `"Did you mean ?"` for `--needs Aa` would pass this test, even though the nearest id is `A` and the promised behavior is to name the nearest real id.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:23

chunk_findings.detail: `_adjust_list(it, edit, fields, "needs")` merges the requested `--add-needs` value with the item’s existing needs into `fields["needs"]`, and `IT.unknown_needs` is then called on that merged list. An item created before this fix may already contain an unknown need (the old code accepted it), so a valid command such as `ddflow task update T --add-needs REAL` will fail with `"no such id 'NOPE'"`, where `NOPE` is the pre-existing invalid dependency, not an ID supplied by this update. The check should validate only the newly supplied `--needs`/`--add-needs` arguments, not the final merged list.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:193-194

chunk_findings.detail: The refusal tests only assert a nonzero exit code and that the unknown id appears in output; none verifies the state was actually refused. For example, an implementation of `task add T --needs NO-SUCH-ID` that prints `NO-SUCH-ID`, returns 1, but still creates `T` would pass `test_task_add_refuses_an_unknown_need`, so the regression test does not prove the dependent task was not filed and the original bug can remain in a weaker form.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:19

chunk_findings.detail: `test_task_add_names_the_nearest_real_id` only checks the string `"Did you mean"`, not the suggested id. With the input `--needs Aa`, an implementation that suggests the wrong real id (`Did you mean B?`) would still pass, even though the intent explicitly requires naming the nearest real id.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:27

chunk_findings.detail: The stated acceptance requires the explicit override to work for `update --needs`/`--add-needs` as well as for `task add`, but the new tests only exercise `--allow-unknown-needs` on `task add`. If the flag is wired only into the add path (for example, `_add.py` honors it while the update command/`_edit.py` does not), `ddflow update T --needs A,NOPE --allow-unknown-needs` would still refuse the command, yet this test file would pass because no test invokes `update` with the override flag. This leaves the promised update override behavior untested.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:test_allow_unknown_needs_overrides_the_refusal

chunk_findings.detail: The only override test exercises `task add --allow-unknown-needs`. The acceptance criteria require the explicit override for both `task add` and `task update --needs`/`--add-needs`. There is no test for `ddflow task update T --add-needs GHOST --allow-unknown-needs` (or `update T --needs GHOST --allow-unknown-needs`), so an implementation that wires the flag only into `task add` would leave the update override path broken while the suite stays green.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:test_allow_unknown_needs_overrides_the_refusal

chunk_findings.detail: The pre-existing-unknown-id regression is only covered for `update --add-needs`. There is no analogous test for `update T --needs A` when `T` already holds an unknown id. That means a `--needs` replacement path that still validates or merges the item’s current needs, rather than only the ids supplied in this update, would refuse a valid command such as `ddflow task update T --needs A` for old items containing `OLD-GHOST`, and the current tests would not catch it.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:test_add_needs_valid_id_is_not_refused_on_a_pre_existing_unknown_need

chunk_findings.detail: The two update refusal tests were rewritten to use the near-miss id `"Aa"` instead of the genuinely unknown id `"GHOST"`. By replacing rather than augmenting, the suite no longer exercises `update --add-needs` or `update --needs` with an id that has no close match. An implementation that correctly suggests `"A"` for `"Aa"` but still silently accepts (or fails to refuse) a completely unknown id such as `"GHOST"` would pass these tests, leaving the original silent-acceptance bug latent for the no-match case.

chunk_findings.detail: Both update near-match refusal tests create task `T` with `--needs A` and then supply the typo `Aa`, whose nearest real id is also `A`. Because `A` is already in `T.needs`, the assertion `_items(repo)["T"].needs == ["A"]` cannot distinguish a true refusal from an implementation that auto-corrects `Aa` to `A`, mutates the task, prints `Did you mean 'A'`, and exits 1. For example, if the code treated an unknown near-match as “did you mean X? I’ll use X” and applied it, these tests would still pass (after deduplication) even though the acceptance criterion requires the command to refuse and leave the task unchanged. To prove refusal, the near-match case should target a real id that is not already a need, e.g. `update T --add-needs Ba` when `T` only needs `A`; the expected `needs` would stay `["A"]` and the hint should name `B`, so an auto-correction would be caught as `["A", "B"]`.

data.summary: The wave/orchestrator lane-fill loop just does ddflow_next -> claim with no explicit selection policy, so interrupted recoveries, open bugs, and phase-less tasks are not promoted ahead of generic ready items. Applies to both kimi and generic reviewer configurations.

data.summary: The cross-family reviewers hit quota walls (kimi 5-hour limit -> HTTP 403, gemini key 403, qwen truncation) and are manually swapped by hand. There is no automatic failover/shedding: govern.quota_mark_* exists but is not wired to reviewer selection, so when the only fast cross-family reviewer exhausts, every rubber_duck/critic gate stalls until a human edits reviewers.toml. Add budget/quota-aware reviewer selection + automatic failover among enabled reviewers (and surface it rather than silently recording unavailable).
